1:
Word of the rebuilding reaches Samaria, and the witnesses gather first around the enemy's rage before they weigh his taunts. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the reflection cast on the Jews as first a thing of the heart: Sanballat and Tobiah were very angry and had great indignation, out of all patience that Nehemiah should come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel, as they had already resented at Neh. 2:10. They had pleased themselves with the thought that while Jerusalem lay unwalled they might swallow it up and make themselves masters of it when they pleased; but a walled city would be first fenced against them and by degrees formidable to them. "The strength and safety of the church," Henry observes, "are the grief and vexation of its enemies." From the heart the malice passed into word: they despised the work and made it the subject of ridicule; and in that very scorn, Henry notes, God brought good out of evil, for reckoning the undertaking a foolish thing that would sink under its own weight, they did not trouble to obstruct it until it was too late.

The reformed John Gill fixes the tense with care. Sanballat heard that "we builded the wall" — or rather were building it, Gill insists, for as yet it was not finished; the enemy's fury is kindled not by an accomplished fact but by a work barely begun, which is what makes his haste to mock so revealing. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a characteristic observation on the writer's method: when the verse says Sanballat "mocked the Jews," the mockery itself comes afterwards; here, as often in Nehemiah, a general statement is made which is then expanded in the verses that follow. The bare notice of derision is the heading; the actual jeers of Sanballat and Tobiah are set down next.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke surveys the whole campaign the chapter will unfold — the mockery meant to prevent the completing of the wall, then the conspiracy to fight, then the countermeasures of prayer and the watch — and draws the abiding lesson that the enemies of God's work endeavour by every means to discredit and destroy it and those employed in it, beginning always by despising the workmen. The witnesses do not divide. Together they show a work of God so slight in its beginnings that its adversaries thought contempt enough to kill it, and a people whose very feebleness became, under God, their protection, since scorn kept the enemy idle while the wall rose.
2:
The jeer itself now sounds, and the witnesses attend both to the audience Sanballat courted and to the sting in each of his questions. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that he vented his anger publicly, "before his brethren" — the rulers of his people — and "the army of Samaria," the host at his command, so that the ridicule was staged before associates and subordinates alike. Keil parses the taunt as a string of present-tense questions, "What are these feeble Jews doing? will they leave it to themselves? will they sacrifice? will they finish it to-day? will they revive the stones out of the heaps that are burned?" The rare word for "feeble," he observes, meaning withered and powerless, occurs here only; and he rejects the older gloss that would make the neighbouring nations the ones expected to "leave them alone," holding the four scoffing questions to share one contemptuous subject.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the audience and the tactics. Adam Clarke, noting that as governor Sanballat commanded the army, sees him working to excite the soldiers against Nehemiah, and reads the whole verse as a textbook of hostility: the enemies of God's work despise the workmen ("what do these feeble Jews?"), turn all into ridicule, have recourse to lying, and sometimes to fair but deceitful speeches such as those at Neh. 6:2. John Wesley catches the mockery of the timescale — "in a day," as though they meant to begin and finish the whole work in a single day — and of the materials, whether they would pick their broken stones out of the ruins and patch them together, stones burnt and shattered by the Chaldeans when they took the city.

The reformed John Gill names the company Sanballat spoke before as Tobiah, Geshem the Arabian, and perhaps other Persian governors of those parts. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott identifies the same hearers as the counsellors and body-guard of Sanballat, warns that "contempt is not scrupulous or precise" in its phrasing, and fastens on the clause "will they sacrifice?" as the very thing Nehemiah will call, in his prayer, the provoking of God before the builders at v.5. The witnesses converge: a cornered governor turns his impotence into theatre, mocking the workers, the work, the time, and the stones, and in mocking the Jews' hope of again offering sacrifice mocks, without knowing it, the God whose house they served.
3:
Tobiah stands at Sanballat's elbow and adds his own jest, and the witnesses read the moment as the pairing of two scoffers who complete each other. The reformed John Gill fixes the man and his place: Tobiah the Ammonite was by him, one of the very brethren before whom Sanballat had just spoken, so that the taunt is not a private aside but a second voice raised in the same public derision. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the character of the sneer. Where Sanballat had scorned the workmen, Tobiah scorns the work itself; he too must have his jest and show his wit, saying that they were likely to make sorry work of it, and would themselves be ashamed of it — for "if a fox go up," not with his subtlety but merely with his weight, "he shall even break down their stone wall."

Henry hears in the exchange a law of the scoffing temper: "profane scoffers sharpen one another." The malice of the one whets the malice of the other, and men who agree in almost nothing else will unite readily enough in mocking a good work. It is a thing to be marked, he says, that many a good work has been looked upon with contempt by proud and haughty scorners; the flimsiness Tobiah imputes to the rising wall is the flimsiness the worldly mind always fancies it sees in the labours of the godly, measuring the church's undertakings by the eye of scorn rather than by the strength of the God who owns them.

The bare notice of Tobiah's presence carries more weight than its brevity suggests. He is named an Ammonite, an old and hereditary enemy of Israel, and his gibe about the fox is meant to reduce the whole enterprise to a heap so weak that a passing animal could topple it. Yet the witnesses let the irony stand unspoken in the record itself: the wall these men reckoned fit to fall under a fox's tread would, before the chapter closed, stand joined to half its height and be defended by armed men, while their confident contempt came to nothing. Gill fixes the fact of Tobiah's part in the mockery, and Henry the disposition behind it — the ready alliance of scoffers, the reflexive scorn of good work — and together they leave a portrait of derision that looks formidable in the moment and foolish in the outcome. The reproach is loud; the wall goes up regardless.
4:
Stung by the derision but disdaining to answer it, Nehemiah turns from the scoffers to God, and the witnesses watch him make of insult an occasion of prayer. The reformed John Gill marks that to the men themselves he sent no answer at all, but applied to the Lord: "Hear, O our God; for we are despised." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the whole committal — Nehemiah lays the matter before God, entreating him to hear how the Jews were become a scorn, to turn the enemies' reproach upon their own head, and to give them for a plunder in a land of captivity, where they would themselves dwell as captives. John Wesley reads that last petition simply: give them for a prey to their enemies, and let those carry them away into captivity.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the pattern for imitation and marks its limit. That Nehemiah begs God to take notice of the indignities done his people is a thing we may follow — God's people have often been a despised people, and it is their comfort that God hears all the slights put upon them, so that they may be, as the psalmist was, as though they were deaf. But when Nehemiah goes on to pray that the reproach be turned back and the sin not covered, Henry judges this spoken "rather by a spirit of prophecy than by a spirit of prayer," and not to be imitated by us who are taught by Christ to pray for those who despitefully use us — for Christ himself prayed for those that reproached him, "Father, forgive them," at Luke 23:34.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the same caution more sharply: a prayer of this kind, understood literally, "is not lawful for any Christian," since our great Master has said, love your enemies and pray for them that despitefully use you, as at Matt. 5:44; such sayings are excusable only in the mouth of a Jew under severe irritation. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, without excusing, describes: it is Nehemiah's habit to turn everything as he goes into devotion, and this prayer is full of an angry jealousy for the honour of a jealous God — a tone of holy revenge that "pervades the Old Testament, and has not altogether departed in the New." The witnesses agree that the appeal to God is right and good; they begin here to divide only over the imprecation that follows it, the fuller weighing of which belongs to the next verse.
5:
The prayer sharpens into imprecation — "cover not their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before thee" — and here the witnesses openly divide over how such words may be understood and whether they may be prayed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch first fix the sense: to ask that the sin be not blotted out is to ask that it not remain unpunished, and the ground alleged is that the enemies "have provoked thee to anger before the builders," openly challenging the wrath of God by despising him where the workmen could hear. The reformed John Gill insists the petition springs "not from a private spirit of revenge, but from a public spirit for the glory of God, and his justice," and reads it less as a curse than as a prophecy of what would surely come to pass, after the manner of many of David's petitions in the Psalms — a reading with warrant, since God had already threatened the Ammonites and Moabites with destruction.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses soften and qualify. Adam Clarke calls these "the most terrible imprecations," but argues they are probably declaratory, the Hebrew verb serving alike as prayer and as prediction, so that the words amount to "their reproach shall be turned, their sin shall not be blotted out"; and he limits their reach to the enemies' bodies and lives, not their souls or the world to come, the whole coming to no more than that what a man sows he shall reap, as at Gal. 6:7. John Wesley reads it as a request that God let their wickedness stand in his sight so far as to bring down judgments upon them, "that either they may be reformed, or others may be warned by their example," God being said to cover sin when he forbears to punish it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry stands with those who will not make it a model. Those who cast contempt on God's people do but prepare everlasting shame for themselves, from which such sinners are seldom recovered; and Nehemiah, he thinks, had reason to judge these hearts desperately hardened, else he would not have prayed the sin might never be blotted out. Henry marks the true spring of the anger: the reason given is not "they have abused us" but "they have provoked thee," and that before the builders; we should be angry at persecutors, he urges, not because their malice is hurtful to us but because it is offensive to God, as the psalmist pleads at Ps. 74:22. So the witnesses circle a real tension without wholly dissolving it — whether the words are a righteous, prophetic declaration for the honour of God, or an utterance of the old dispensation that the Christian, taught to bless his enemies, may not take upon his own lips.
6:
The narrative lifts from the enemies' mouths to the builders' hands, and the witnesses rejoice in the single cause of the work's swift progress. The reformed John Gill notes plainly that they went on building notwithstanding all the scoffs and threats. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe how far the work had come: the Jews continued to build without heeding the ridicule, and "all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof" — that is, so far repaired throughout its whole circumference that no breach or gap was left up to half its height — and they trace the speed to its source, "the people had a heart to work." Charles Ellicott confirms the measure: up to half its height the wall was now continuous.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the emphatic Hebrew, "the people had a heart to work," and draws the lesson that lies in it: where the heart is engaged, the work of God goes on well. He notes as well the curiosity that the whole of this verse is omitted by the Septuagint, so that its record of the builders' zeal survives to us only in the Hebrew. The engaged heart, for Clarke, is the whole secret of the rising wall; the enemies' derision could not touch a people whose affections were fixed upon the work.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers these threads into his account of the builders' vigour. Notwithstanding the reflections cast upon them, they made such good speed that in a little time they had run the wall up to half its height, "for the people had a mind to work; their hearts were upon it, and they would have it forwarded." From this he takes two settled maxims. The first: "good work goes on well when people have a mind to it," the willing heart accomplishing more than any pressure of command. The second turns the enemies' malice on its head: "the reproaches of enemies should rather quicken us to our duty than drive us from it." The scorn of Sanballat and Tobiah, meant to make the builders drop their tools in shame, served instead to spur them; and the witnesses land together on a quiet reversal that runs through the whole chapter — that a work God owns is not slowed by contempt but hastened by it, when the labourers have set their hearts to do his will. The wall at half its height is the visible answer to the jeer that a fox might topple it.
7:
Derision having failed to stop the work, the adversaries turn from mockery to menace, and the witnesses mark the widening of the conspiracy and the wrath that drove it. The reformed John Gill notes the alliance now enlarged — Sanballat, Tobiah, and the Arabians who followed Geshem, joined by Ammonites and Ashdodites. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott together read the occasion: when the enemies heard that the walls of Jerusalem "were made up," risen to the height before mentioned, and that the breaches "began to be stopped," the wall now continuous, they were very wroth. Ellicott adds a sober note of scale — the tribes here enumerated were only small parties under the immediate influence of Sanballat, nothing beyond that being likely among subjects held in common under Persia.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry anatomizes the malice. The conspirators were not Sanballat and Tobiah only but other neighbouring peoples whom they had drawn into the plot; having flattered themselves that the work would stand still of itself, they were, when it prospered, angry at the Jews for being so hasty to push it forward and angry at themselves for being so slow to oppose it. "Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce," Henry cries; nothing would now content them but to fight against Jerusalem. And he probes the root of it: the Jews had done them no wrong and designed them none, but lived peaceably by them; it was merely out of envy and malice, for "they hated the Jews' piety, and were therefore vexed at their prosperity, and sought their ruin."

Henry marks three features of the plot that the verses just ahead will unfold, and finds them all latent in this kindling of wrath: how unanimous the enemies were, conspiring all together though of interests so different among themselves that only opposition to the work of God could have united them; how close and secret, promising themselves success from the privacy of their design; and how cruel, thirsting for the very blood of the builders. The witnesses converge on the reading that the turn from scorn to violence is itself a testimony to the work's success — the enemy laughs while he thinks the wall will fall of its own weight, and only rages when he sees it standing. The rising wall that had provoked a jest now provokes a war; and the same prosperity that vexed the scoffers into silence has stirred a coalition of neighbours, from the Arabians of the south to the Ashdodites of the west, into a common and furious design.
8:
The scattered malice hardens into a single design, and the witnesses weigh both the confederacy and its aim. The reformed John Gill states the fact plainly: all the men and peoples named entered into a confederacy and combination, "conspired all of them together." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds two pointed observations. First, on the boldness of the plot: not fearing the Persian authority under which they all lived as subjects, they resolved to attack the city — though, he notes with the vantage of one who reads to the chapter's end, "it will be seen that they soon abandoned that project." Second, on the wording: the phrase our version renders "to hinder it" is better read "to do it hurt," so that the purpose is not merely obstruction but injury — harm meant against Jerusalem and its builders.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the character of the combination in three strokes. First, its unanimity: they conspired all together, though of different and even rival interests among themselves, made one only by their shared opposition to the work of God — a grim unity in which men who could agree in nothing else agree in this. Second, its secrecy: they took crafty counsel and "digged deep to hide it from the Lord," saying within themselves that the Jews should not know nor see till they had them at their mercy, and promising themselves security and success from the very closeness of their management. Third, its cruelty: nothing less than "we will come and slay them" would serve, and they were glad of any pretence to shed the blood they thirsted for.

Yet Henry sets over the whole a confidence that undoes it. The design was to cause the good work to cease, and of this the enemies were fully assured; but "the hindering of good work is that which bad men aim at and promise themselves — but good work is God's work, and it shall prosper." The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the fact of the league, Ellicott its rashness against Persia and its malicious aim, Henry its unholy unanimity, secrecy, and bloodthirst; and together they let the reader see a formidable coalition, confident of surprise, arrayed against a half-built wall — a coalition that, for all its rage and craft, is already reckoned by the historian among the counsels that God will bring to nought. The threat is real and the danger near; but the outcome, the witnesses agree, was never in the conspirators' hands.
9:
Against the threat of a surprise attack Nehemiah joins two things the witnesses are careful never to separate: he prays, and he posts a guard. The reformed John Gill reads the first clause as the spreading of the whole case before God in prayer, entreating direction and help. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the second: "because of them" is rather "over against them," the watch set opposite to each point of the enemy's encampment, and this setting of the guard, he notes, was accompanied by solemn and united prayer — the two acts done together, not one instead of the other.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke makes the verse a small treatise on the concord of faith and means. "The strongest confidence in the protection and favour of God does not preclude the use of all or any of the means of self-preservation and defence which his providence has put in our power." While God works in us both to will and to do, as at Phil. 2:12-13, we must yet proceed to willing through the power he gives us to will, and to action through the power he gives us to act; the power and the use of it, Clarke insists, are two distinct things, so that a man may have the power to act and yet not act. Seeing God has wrought these powers in us, the apostle's charge holds — work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into a rule of Christian prudence, drawing on the Lord's own words. Nehemiah first "looked up, engaged God for him," making his prayer before he used any means, "for with him we must always begin"; and all his cares and griefs and fears he spread before God, and thereby made himself easy. Then, having prayed, he set a watch. The instructions of Christ in our spiritual warfare agree exactly with the example, Henry observes, at Matt. 26:41: watch and pray. "If we think to secure ourselves by prayer only, without watchfulness, we are slothful and tempt God; if by watchfulness, without prayer, we are proud and slight God; and, either way, we forfeit his protection." The witnesses do not divide; Gill, Ellicott, Clarke, and Henry weave one cord — that trust in God and diligent use of means are not rivals but partners, and that the man who both kneels and keeps guard has done all a believer ought.
10:
At the very moment the enemy plots a surprise, a graver danger rises within the walls — the failing spirit of the builders themselves. The reformed John Gill attributes the complaint to several of the men of Judah, and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain what had worn them down: the placing of the watch day and night, added to continuous labour, pressed heavily upon the people, so that Judah said, "The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish; we are not able to build the wall" — in plain terms, the labour is beyond our power, we cannot go on. Adam Clarke fills in the toil behind the words: they worked day and night, scarcely putting off their clothes, and had first to clear away the ruins before they could so much as dig the foundation of a new wall, a labour that had brought them near exhaustion.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the very name "Judah" a significant weight, and treats the verse as the writer's summary of the difficulties: the people complained of their growing feebleness, the more so because so many hands were now diverted to the watches. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the same discouragement — the Jews now dwelling in Judah, partly terrified by their enemies and partly wearied with continual labour, faced rubbish more than they could suddenly remove, and, forced to spend their time clearing it, thought they must desist for a season.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the irony and the lesson. At the very hour the adversaries said, "Let us cause the work to cease," the builders themselves said, "Let us even let it fall, for we are not able to go forward with it." They represented the labourers as tired and the remaining removal of the rubbish as an insuperable difficulty, and so counselled desisting for the present. "Can Judah, that warlike valiant tribe, sneak thus?" Henry marvels; and he turns it to a truth for every leader of good work: "active leading men have many times as much ado to grapple with the fears of their friends as with the terrors of their enemies." The witnesses converge on the sober point that the wall was as much endangered by the weariness within as by the malice without — that discouragement, when the burden is heavy and the rubbish deep, can do the enemy's work for him, and that the same faith which posts a guard against the foe must also hearten the fainting hands of one's own people.
11:
The builders' weariness is compounded by a whisper of the enemy's design, and the witnesses read the boast of the plotters as the very engine of the people's fear. The reformed John Gill glosses the opening simply: "they shall not know" — our designs upon them shall be hidden. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw the connection to the fainting spirits just described: the discouragement of the Jews was increased by the words of their enemies, who said the Jews should not know nor see till the adversaries came into the midst among them, slew them, and caused the work to cease. Charles Ellicott fixes the strategy in the boast: as to the adversaries, their plan was evidently to watch and surprise, rather than to make the open, threatened attack — a stroke meant to fall unseen.

The menace lies in its stealth. The enemies do not now propose a siege in the daylight but an ambush in the dark, a sudden irruption "in the midst" of scattered and unsuspecting workmen, so that the wall should be watered with the blood of its builders before any alarm could be raised. It is precisely the sort of threat calculated to unnerve a tired people already murmuring that they are not able to build; the imagined knife in the night does more to weaken the hands than any host drawn up before the gate.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets over this confident scheming the counter-truth that governs the whole passage. The declared aim of the plot was to cause the work to cease, and of achieving it the enemies were fully confident; but "the hindering of good work is that which bad men aim at and promise themselves — but good work is God's work, and it shall prosper." The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the boast "they shall not know" is at once a real and frightening danger — a surprise that might indeed have cut down the builders — and an empty confidence, since the very secrecy the enemies leaned upon is the thing God is about to overthrow, bringing their whispered counsel to light through the neighbours who will carry word to Jerusalem in the verse that follows. The plotters reckon on being unseen; but there is an eye they have not counted, and a providence that turns their concealed malice into open knowledge before ever the blow can fall.
12:
Word of the danger reaches Nehemiah through the very Jews who lived among the enemies, and the witnesses labour over a sentence that all confess to be obscure. The reformed John Gill sets the scene: Jews dwelling near Samaria, Arabia, and Ashdod, having intelligence of the enemies' designs, came with their warning. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the message as a summons: these neighbours, who had heard the adversaries' words, came to Jerusalem and said ten times — that is, again and again — "from all places ye must return to us," for the enemies were surrounding the community on every side, Sanballat and the Samaritans on the north, the Ammonites on the east, the Arabians on the south, and the Ashdodites on the west. On this reading the outlying Jews were calling their fellow-townsmen home for common safety. Charles Ellicott reads much the same, hearing the neighbours in their terror say by repeated messages, "from all places, ye shall return to us" — that is, for our protection.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the difficulty harder. John Wesley takes the sense to be that the enemies "will invade you every way, by which we can come to you, or you to us," and so counsels watch on every side; he adds that the "ten times" is a round number for an uncertain one, and that these neighbours, though lacking zeal to come and build, had concern enough to warn their brethren. Adam Clarke declares the verse "extremely difficult," observes that our version supplies "they will be upon you" with nothing answering in the Hebrew, and prefers the Septuagint's clear sense, "they come up from all places against us." He inclines further, with Houbigant, Michaelis, and Dath, to a slight emendation — reading a verb that means "they designed or meditated" for the received "ye shall return" — which would yield, "the Jews who dwelt among them told us frequently, from all places, what the enemies designed against us," though he grants that no manuscript and no version supports the change.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the intelligence for its providence rather than its grammar. The Jews that dwelt by the enemies, though without zeal to come up and help build, had honesty and affection enough to give warning, and gave it ten times, as men in earnest and under a concern; the report was expressed abruptly, Henry thinks, as by men out of breath and in confusion, whose very looks made up the deficiency of their words. From it he draws his lesson: "God has many ways of bringing to light, and so bringing to nought, the devices and designs of his and his church's enemies"; even the cold, feeble Jews who dwelt among the foe are made to serve as spies upon them, so that, rather than fail, "a bird of the air shall carry their voice." The witnesses divide over the words but agree on the substance — that the enemies' secret was betrayed, and that the God whom the plotters thought to hide from had ears in their own camp.
13:
Warned of the danger, Nehemiah arrays his people for defence, and the witnesses attend to a verse they candidly find hard to construe. The reformed John Gill takes the plain military sense: Nehemiah set guards in the lower places behind the wall, where it was lowest and the enemy might most easily break it down or climb over. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confess the sentence "hardly intelligible," and render it that he stationed the people at the lowest places behind the wall, at the bare and dried-up spots — open places exposed to the sun, perhaps bare hills, whence approaching foes might be discerned at a distance — setting them there by their families, armed with their swords, their spears, and their bows.

Charles Ellicott works the same knot and identifies the two kinds of position. In allusion to the ambushes threatened, Nehemiah set families together, besides the appointed guards, "in the lower places" where the wall was not yet raised to its due height, and on the "higher" or rather the bare places whence enemies might be better seen; the "lower," he concludes, were the "bare" places. John Wesley reads the arrangement more simply: "behind" means within the walls where they were not yet raised to their full height and so most liable to assault, and the "higher" places are the tops of the walls where they were finished, and the towers built here and there upon them, whence the defenders might shoot arrows or throw down stones.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the tactics and finds a wisdom in them that reaches beyond the stones. In the lower places he set the guards behind the wall, that they might annoy the enemy over it, as from a breastwork; in the higher places, where the wall stood at its full height, he set them upon it, that from the top they might cast down stones or darts on the heads of the assailants. And he marks the human wisdom of the disposition Nehemiah chose: "he set them after their families, that mutual relation might engage them to mutual assistance." Kinsman posted beside kinsman would fight the harder, each defending not a stranger but his own. The witnesses divide only over the obscure geography of "lower" and "bare" and "higher" places; they agree on the substance — that Nehemiah met the threat of a hidden attack by an open readiness, arming his people where the wall was weakest and where the enemy could soonest be spied, and binding them together by the strongest of natural bonds so that the defence of Jerusalem became the defence of every man's own house.
14:
Seeing his people posted yet fearful, Nehemiah rises to hearten them, and the witnesses divide first over what he looked at before they gather around what he said. The reformed John Gill takes "I looked" of a survey of the people — Nehemiah observed that they were in their proper places and sufficiently armed, and watched whether the enemy was coming. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it rather of prayer: he "looked up, engaged God for him, and put himself and his cause under the divine protection," spreading all his cares and griefs and fears before God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes it of the crisis itself, holding that this energetic appeal was uttered on the actual approach of an attacking party. The witnesses read the one word three ways — a glance at his own ranks, a glance upward to heaven, a glance at the advancing foe.

On the address they converge. Keil and Delitzsch give it whole: seeing the people so placed, Nehemiah said to the nobles, the rulers, and the rest, "Be not afraid of them; remember the Lord, the great and the terrible," who will fight for them as he promised at Deut. 20:3, "and fight ye for your brethren, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your houses." Adam Clarke turns the exhortation into a challenge — are the enemies more terrible or stronger than God? — and reads the appeal as a call to fight for all that is dear: countrymen who worship the same God, sons the enemy would slay, daughters and wives they would defile, houses they would seize. A people so interested, fighting for their altars and their hearths, "can never be conquered"; and he sets beside it the like harangue in Aeschylus, "Sons of the Greeks, go on! Free now your country, and your children free."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds the whole encouragement built on two supports — whom they fought under and whom they fought for. Observing even the nobles and rulers in consternation, their hands weakened for work and war, Nehemiah bids them consider their captain: "Remember the Lord, who is great and terrible; you think your enemies great and terrible, but what are they in comparison with God?" Those who see the church's God great and terrible, Henry says, will see the church's enemies mean and despicable, for "the reigning fear of God is the best antidote against the ensnaring fear of man"; he that is afraid of a man that shall die forgets the Lord his Maker, as at Isa. 51:12-13. And then their cause: they fought for their brethren, their sons and daughters, as the psalmist pleaded "for my brethren's sake" at Ps. 122:8 — all that was dear to them lying at stake. The witnesses leave the fainting builders steadied between a God too great to fear beside and a household too dear to lose.
15:
The threatened blow never falls, and the witnesses read the enemies' retreat as the quiet undoing of a plot that had leaned wholly on secrecy. The reformed John Gill notes that the adversaries heard their design was known, gathered from the preparations the Jews had made to receive and defend themselves. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw the whole movement together: the design of the enemy being circumvented, the Jews returned to the work on the wall which they had forsaken to take up their weapons, and from this point they laboured in a new manner — one half working while the other half stood in arms. Charles Ellicott admires the compression of the record, which "remarkably condenses the frustration of the attempt and the cessation of the special guard" into a single sentence.

Adam Clarke fastens on one word with an eye to an earlier crux: the text says God "had brought their counsel to nought," and the very term "counsel" here, he suggests, countenances the emendation he had proposed at the difficult verse a little before, where he would read that the neighbours reported what the enemies had counselled or designed. The frustrated "counsel" of this verse thus reads back, for Clarke, upon the obscure warning that first exposed it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the happy disappointment. When the enemies found their design discovered and the Jews upon their guard, they concluded it to no purpose to attempt anything, "but that God had brought their counsel to nought"; for they knew they could gain their point only by surprise, and once the plot was known it was quashed. Thereupon the Jews returned every one to his work, and with so much the more cheerfulness because they now saw plainly that God owned the work and owned them in the doing of it. From this Henry takes his settled note: "God's care of our safety should engage and encourage us to go on with vigour in our duty. As soon as ever a danger is over let us return to our work, and trust God another time." The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the cause of the enemies' withdrawal, Keil the return to a guarded labour, Ellicott the terseness of the record, Clarke the telltale word "counsel," and Henry the joy and the lesson; together they show a conspiracy of surprise defeated the moment it ceased to be secret, and a people sent back to their trowels heartened by the visible care of God.
16:
From this day the work goes on under arms, and the witnesses describe the standing arrangement Nehemiah now instituted. The reformed John Gill dates it from the time they were alarmed of danger. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the division: from that day half of Nehemiah's servants wrought at the work while the other half held the spears, the shields, the bows, and the coats of mail; the "servants," they explain, are his personal retinue, the Jews placed at his disposal as governor, and "the rulers were behind all the house of Judah," posted to support the whole body. Charles Ellicott distinguishes carefully: Nehemiah's own servants, marked off from "all the house of Judah," were split into two parties, one building and one bearing arms; the habergeons are coats of mail or corselets, thin plates of metal sewn upon leather; and the rulers stood behind, ready to lead the defence if it came.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fill in the picture. Adam Clarke observes that such a practice is no strange thing even now in Palestine, where men sowing their seed are attended by an armed guard against the robbing Arabs, and glosses the habergeon as a coat of mail, or rather a breastplate to cover the chest. John Wesley reads the measure as a precaution renewed "lest our enemies should repeat their enterprise": half of the domestic servants and guards stood in their arms, prepared for battle, while the rulers were behind to encourage the workers, sometimes to lend their own hands, and to command in case of an assault — the "house of Judah" being the Jews at labour upon the wall.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the spiritual pattern in the arrangement. When the builders returned to their work they were not so secure as to lay down their arms, knowing how restless and unwearied their enemies were, and how, if one design failed, they would be hatching another; "thus must we watch always against our spiritual enemies, and not expect that our warfare will be accomplished till our work is." While one half were at work the other half were under arms, holding spears and shields and bows not only for themselves but for the labourers, who could catch up their weapons at the first alarm; and Henry supposes they changed services at stated hours, which relieved the fatigue of both and eased especially the bearers of burdens whose strength had decayed. So they divided their time between the trowels and the spears. The witnesses converge on a single image — a wall built with weapons at hand, a people who could neither labour without watching nor watch without labouring, and in whom Henry finds the very portrait of the Christian, at once a builder and a soldier all his days.
17:
The verse pictures every worker doubly employed, and the witnesses take opposite views of how literally to press the image. The reformed John Gill describes the builders as those who laid the mortar and the stones and the timber where it was needed. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott divides the labourers into masons and their burden-bearers, and reads the verse precisely: the burden-bearers held in one hand a weapon while they carried with the other, whereas the masons, needing both hands, built with both and had their weapons laid at their side. On this reading the "one hand" belongs strictly to the carriers, not the builders.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses and the puritan-evangelical Henry take the expression as figurative. Adam Clarke reads it that each man "had his arms at hand, and was as fully prepared to fight as to work," and illustrates from Ovid's Canace, who says one hand holds the pen and the other the sword — not that she wrote with a blade in her grip, but that the weapon lay ready. John Wesley calls it plainly "a proverbial speech, as when they say of a man pretending kindness, he carries bread in one hand, and a stone in another," and turns it to the soul's warfare: "thus must we work out our salvation, with the weapons of our warfare in our hands, for in every duty we must expect opposition from our spiritual enemies." Matthew Henry agrees that the words cannot be understood strictly, "for the work would require both hands," but intimate that the builders were equally employed in both labour and defence.

So a genuine, if modest, difference runs beneath the shared picture. Ellicott would keep something literal in the phrase — the burden-bearer truly grasping a weapon as he carried — while Clarke, Wesley, and Henry hear a proverb for armed readiness rather than a description of one-handed masonry. None of them lets the difference obscure the point on which all agree, which the same Wesley and Henry press hardest: that the verse has become, for the church, an emblem of the whole Christian life. Every believer, Henry says, is both a labourer and a soldier, working with one hand and fighting with the other; the building of the wall and the guarding of it go forward together, and the servant of God is never permitted to lay down either the trowel or the sword. The witnesses leave the reader with a workman who is a warrior, and a warrior who does not cease to build — the daily task pursued with the weapons of its defence always within reach.
18:
The single detail this verse adds — the sword girded at every builder's side and the trumpeter beside Nehemiah — the witnesses read as the perfecting of a defence that never interrupts the work. The reformed John Gill notes that each of the builders had his sword girded on, and so built; thus accoutred he wrought, prepared in a moment for either service, the mason's or the soldier's. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fixes the office of the trumpet: it was sounded "to call the people together, when, and where it was necessary" — the one signal by which a labour spread thin along the wall could be gathered in an instant.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on both particulars and lifts each into a spiritual figure. Every builder had a sword by his side, a weapon he could carry without hindering his labour, worn ready so that he need never lay down his work to look for it. And in that Henry finds the great emblem: "the word of God is the sword of the Spirit," as the apostle names it at Eph. 6:17, "which we ought to have always at hand and never to seek, both in our labours and in our conflicts as Christians." The believer's Scripture, like the builder's sword, is not a thing to be fetched in the hour of assault but a thing already girded on, carried through every ordinary task so as to be instantly drawn when the tempter or the adversary strikes.

Henry marks too the care Nehemiah took to have early notice of any attack: he kept a trumpeter always by him, to sound an alarm upon the first intimation of danger, so that a work carried on at many separated points might yet act as one body at need. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the plain fact of the girded sword and the readiness it gave, Wesley the summoning purpose of the trumpet, and Henry the double lesson that arms and alarm together teach — that the servant of God works best who works armed, and that the scattered labourers of the church are kept safe not by their own vigilance only but by a watchman set to warn them and a signal appointed to draw them together. The sword at the side and the trumpet at the leader's hand make of a long, exposed, and vulnerable line a single defended whole, every man building yet every man ready, and all of them one at the sound of the horn.
19:
Nehemiah explains to the leaders and the people the reason for the trumpet, and the witnesses read his words as the wise provision of a commander whose forces are dangerously dispersed. The reformed John Gill marks simply that he said this to the nobles, the rulers, and the rest of the people — the same charge given to all who were employed in the building. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the substance: "The work is great and large, and we are separated upon the wall one far from another; in what place ye hear the sound of the trumpet, assemble yourselves to me: our God will fight for us." The danger, that is, lay precisely in the scale of the undertaking. A wall encircling the whole city meant a workforce strung out at intervals, each company out of reach of the next, and so open to being cut off and overwhelmed piecemeal before help could come.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out how Nehemiah met that peril of dispersion. The work was large and the builders were spread abroad, for in all parts of the wall they were labouring at the same time; and Nehemiah continually walked round to oversee the work and to encourage the workmen, so that he might have the speediest intelligence if the enemy made an attack, and by sound of trumpet give notice to all at once. The commander's own restless circuit of the wall and the single agreed signal together bound the scattered parties into one.

Henry does not let the martial arrangement stand without its comfort. The summons to gather at the trumpet's call ends not in the men's own valour but in a promise: "our God will fight for us." The believers were to run to the point of danger, but they ran under the assurance that the battle was the Lord's; the rallying of the workmen was the human side of a defence whose strength lay in God. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the audience, Keil the words and the danger they answer, Henry the leader's vigilance and the promise that crowns the plan; and together they leave a picture of a great and exposed work made safe by three things held together — a watchful leader ever going the rounds, a clear signal that could summon the whole, and above them both the confidence that God himself would fight for a people gathered in his name to build his city.
20:
The instruction of the trumpet is now made explicit, and the witnesses read in it both a shrewd tactic and a confession of faith. The reformed John Gill notes the reach of the order: at whatever part of the wall a man might be working, even the most distant, he was to run to the sound. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the command and its ground together — "resort ye thither unto us: our God shall fight for us" — the summons to converge and the promise that upholds it set side by side.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke explains the military necessity the arrangement answered. Because the walls were very extensive and the workmen consequently much scattered, their enemies might easily fall upon them and destroy them one company after another; Nehemiah therefore ordered them all to work as near to one another as they could, and himself, everywhere surveying the work, kept a trumpeter constantly with him, who was to sound when the enemy approached, so that all were instantly to run to the place from which the alarm came. The dispersion that made the work possible was also its weakness, and the trumpet was the remedy that could knit the scattered line into a single fighting body at a moment's need.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the shift the alarm required of the builders. Upon the first intimation of danger the trumpet would sound, and the people were to repair to Nehemiah, and to do so "with a full assurance that their God would fight for them." When they acted as workmen it was requisite that they be dispersed wherever there was work to do; but when they acted as soldiers it was requisite that they come into close order and be found together in a body. Thus, Henry adds, "should the labourers in Christ's building be ready to unite against a common foe." The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the universality of the summons, Keil the union of tactic and trust, Clarke the strategy of a scattered force gathered by a signal, and Henry the passage from dispersed labour to concentrated defence; and all of them let the promise carry the weight of the verse — that the running together of the workmen was but the visible motion of a defence whose real strength was that God himself had undertaken to fight for the builders of Jerusalem.
21:
The verse sums up the labour and measures its length, and the witnesses find in that measure the whole strain and steadiness of the enterprise. The reformed John Gill notes the continuing division of the workforce — they laboured in the work while half of them held the spears and the other weapons named before. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the sentence as a general recapitulation, with the added and telling note of the length of the day's work during this pressing season: labour that ran from the first light of morning until the stars came out.

That span from dawn to dark is the heart of the verse, and the witnesses feel its weight. The builders did not divide the day between work and rest but gave the whole of it, and more than the whole of the daylight, to the wall; and the armed half stood their guard across the same long hours, so that neither the trowel nor the spear was ever wholly laid down while light or even twilight lasted. It is a picture of men spending themselves without reserve, the weariness lamented earlier in the chapter now borne through the longest of days because the work would not wait and the enemy would not sleep.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out both the tactic and the lesson in the lifted spears. They were held up, he observes, with the very sight of them meant to terrify the enemy, and that not only from sun to sun but "from twilight to twilight every day." And in this unremitting vigilance he finds the pattern of the believer's watch: "thus ought we to be always upon our guard against our spiritual enemies, not only while it is light, but when it is dark," for our adversaries are the rulers of the darkness of this world, as the apostle warns at Eph. 6:12. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the standing division of labour and arms, Ellicott the recapitulation and the extraordinary length of the working day, Henry the terror of the raised spears and the spiritual counsel of a watch that outlasts the daylight; and together they leave the builders bent to their task from the rising of the morning till the stars appeared, weapons gleaming through the dusk, a people who had learned that the work of God asks not a measured portion of the day but the whole of a man's strength and waking hours.
22:
To the day's guard Nehemiah adds a provision for the night, and the witnesses commend the prudence of it. The reformed John Gill notes that he said this to the people at work upon the wall. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the order and its purpose: let every one with his servant lodge within Jerusalem, remaining together through the night rather than scattering across the surrounding district, "that they may be a guard to us in the night, and labour in the day" — the very words for watch and work standing, they note, for the watchers and the workers themselves.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke explains the change of habit the danger forced. The country people were accustomed, after their day's labour, to return to their homes and families; but now, so formidably threatened, Nehemiah obliged them all to sleep in Jerusalem, that they might be ready, in case of a night attack, to help their brethren. Clarke's verdict on the whole set of measures is warm: "all this man's arrangements were wise and judicious." What might have seemed a hardship — keeping labourers from their own beds and households — was in truth a shrewd concentration of force, turning a workforce that dispersed each evening into a garrison that held the city through the dark.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the point into a maxim. The inhabitants of the villages were ordered to lodge within Jerusalem with their servants, not only that they might be the nearer to their work in the morning but that they might be ready to help if an attack came in the night. And from it Henry draws his rule: "the strength of a city lies more in its hands than in its walls; secure them, and God's blessing upon them, and be secure." A wall, however high, is only as safe as the men who man it; better a defended breach than an unguarded rampart. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the audience, Keil the order and its double duty of watch by night and work by day, Clarke the wisdom of overriding the labourers' custom for the common safety, and Henry the truth that a city's real bulwark is its people; and together they show a leader who thought not only how to build the wall but how to keep it, gathering his whole force behind the gates so that Jerusalem should never lie, even for a night, unmanned.
23:
The chapter closes on the total devotion of Nehemiah and his household, who scarcely undressed through the whole pressing season, and the witnesses honour the diligence even as they wrestle with a stubbornly obscure last clause. The reformed John Gill marks the company — neither Nehemiah, nor his brethren the nobles and rulers, nor his servants, nor the men of the guard that followed him put off their clothes. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm that they were constantly in their garments, never putting them off to rest, and confess the closing words, which read literally "every one his weapon water," to be very obscure and to yield no tolerable sense as they stand, so that various emendations have been proposed to recover the meaning.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the whole tangle of the versions. The bare Hebrew, he shows, can be rendered word for word "a man his dart to the waters," which makes little sense; the Vulgate has "every one stripped himself for the bath," the Septuagint omits the clause, the Syriac reads that none put off his clothes "for a month, each in his turn." Clarke judges most likely a reading he found in one manuscript of De Rossi's, which would give, "we did not lay aside our garments, but in order to send them to the washing" — the general meaning being that they worked almost day and night, took their rest by turns, and put off their clothes only when these had to be washed. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds our version's "saving that every one put them off for washing" very improbable, since the words are simply "every man his weapon water"; rejecting as too subtle the notion that "each man's weapon was his water," he thinks it best to supply the ellipsis and read, "every man went with his weapon to the water" — keeping his arms about him even when he went to drink or to wash. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the plainer sense of our text, that the clothes were put off only when they were to wash and cleanse themselves from some impurity that might befall them or their garments.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets aside the philology to weigh the devotion. So intent was Nehemiah upon the work, and so closely did he hold his servants to it, that while the heat of the business lasted neither he nor his attendants went into bed, but every night lay and slept in their clothes, except that they shifted them now and then for cleanliness or in a case of ceremonial pollution. "It was a sign that their heart was upon their work," Henry says, "when they could not find time to dress and undress"; and he draws the abiding lesson that "good work is likely to go on successfully when those that labour in it thus make a business of it." The witnesses divide over the last hard words — whether they speak of clothes sent to the wash or of a man carrying his weapon to the water — but they close in one accord upon the picture the verse was meant to leave: a governor and his men so given to the building of God's city that they lay down armed and rose up armed, and counted the labour worth the surrender of their very rest.
